misconceptions.statement: There is plenty of water on Earth, so we can never run out of usable water.
misconceptions.why: Students see that most of Earth is covered by water and assume all of it is usable.
misconceptions.fix: Most of Earth's water is salty sea water; only about 3% is fresh and much of that is frozen or deep underground, so usable water is limited.

probe.question: Earth is mostly water. Can people ever face a shortage of usable water?
probe.wrong_answer: No, there is so much water that it can never run short.

misconceptions.root_belief: big total means everything is available for use
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of children's ideas about the water cycle and water resources

misconceptions.statement: About half of the water on Earth is fresh water that we can drink.
misconceptions.why: Students guess a large share because water looks abundant everywhere.
misconceptions.fix: About 97% of Earth's water is salty and only about 3% is fresh, and most of that is not easily reachable.

probe.question: Roughly what share of Earth's water is fresh?
probe.wrong_answer: About half of it.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

misconceptions.statement: Rivers and lakes hold most of the fresh water on Earth.
misconceptions.why: Rivers and lakes are the water students see, so they assume it is the main store.
misconceptions.fix: Most fresh water is locked in glaciers and ice caps or lies underground; rivers and lakes hold only a tiny part.

probe.question: Where is most of the Earth's fresh water stored?
probe.wrong_answer: In rivers and lakes.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students' ideas of where water is found on Earth

misconceptions.statement: Sea water can be used for drinking and irrigation if we have a lot of it.
misconceptions.why: Students think quantity makes up for quality.
misconceptions.fix: Salt in sea water harms the body and crops, so it must be desalinated first, which is costly.

probe.question: A village near the sea has no fresh water. Can it simply drink and irrigate with sea water?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, sea water is water and can be used directly.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: Rain refills all our water, so there is no need to save water.
misconceptions.why: Students see rain every year and think supply is automatically restored.
misconceptions.fix: Rain is uneven and much runs off or evaporates; our use, especially of groundwater, can exceed what rain refills, so saving is needed.

probe.question: Since it rains every monsoon, do we still need to save water?
probe.wrong_answer: No, the rain will refill everything again.

misconceptions.root_belief: nature always restores what we use
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of children's ideas on renewable resources

misconceptions.statement: Every part of India gets about the same amount of rain.
misconceptions.why: Students generalise from the rain in their own area.
misconceptions.fix: Rainfall differs widely: Meghalaya gets very heavy rain while western Rajasthan gets very little.

probe.question: Does Jaisalmer get as much rain as Cherrapunji?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, all parts of India get similar rain.

misconceptions.root_belief: my local experience applies everywhere

misconceptions.statement: All the rain that falls on the ground becomes drinking water.
misconceptions.why: Students link rain directly to water supply without thinking about losses.
misconceptions.fix: Much rain flows away in drains and rivers to the sea, evaporates, or gets polluted, so only part becomes usable unless it is collected or soaks in.

probe.question: In a city with paved roads, does all rain become usable water?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, all of it turns into drinking water.

misconceptions.root_belief: one step is the whole process

misconceptions.statement: Groundwater is a big underground lake or river.
misconceptions.why: Pictures and the word underground water suggest a pool of water beneath the ground.
misconceptions.fix: Groundwater fills tiny gaps in soil, sand and rock, like water in a wet sponge.

probe.question: What does groundwater look like under the ground?
probe.wrong_answer: A large lake or river flowing underground.

misconceptions.root_belief: unseen things look like familiar visible things
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of students' conceptions of groundwater

misconceptions.statement: The water table is a fixed level that never changes.
misconceptions.why: Students picture the water table as a permanent line in the diagram.
misconceptions.fix: The water table rises after rain and recharge and falls when much water is pumped out or when it is dry.

probe.question: Can the water table go up or down?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it always stays at the same depth.

misconceptions.root_belief: diagrams show things that never change

misconceptions.statement: Groundwater refills as fast as we pump it, so it can never run out.
misconceptions.why: Students assume nature restores resources at the rate they are used.
misconceptions.fix: Recharge through soil is slow, taking years, so heavy pumping can drain groundwater faster than it refills.

probe.question: If farmers pump many borewells, will the groundwater refill at once?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it refills as fast as we take it.

misconceptions.root_belief: nature always restores what we use
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of misconceptions about renewable resources and groundwater

misconceptions.statement: If a borewell is dry, there is no more water anywhere below that area.
misconceptions.why: Students think a dry well shows the groundwater is totally gone, or the opposite, that a deeper well always fixes it.
misconceptions.fix: A dry borewell shows the water table has fallen below its depth; digging deeper may reach water for a while but it speeds up depletion.

probe.question: A borewell goes dry. What is the best long-term solution?
probe.wrong_answer: Dig a much deeper borewell; water will always be found.

misconceptions.root_belief: digging deeper always solves the problem

misconceptions.statement: Rainwater harvesting is only useful in places that get very heavy rain.
misconceptions.why: Students think collecting water only makes sense where there is plenty.
misconceptions.fix: Harvesting helps even in dry areas, because it stores scarce rain that would otherwise be lost, as in Rajasthan's johads and tankas.

probe.question: Is rainwater harvesting useful in a low-rainfall area?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only heavy-rain places need it.

misconceptions.root_belief: more resource means more need to manage it

misconceptions.statement: Harvested rainwater is useful only for storing in tanks, not for refilling groundwater.
misconceptions.why: Students picture harvesting as only roof tanks.
misconceptions.fix: Recharge pits, trenches and percolation tanks let rain soak into the ground and raise the water table.

probe.question: How can rain collected in a pit help wells nearby?
probe.wrong_answer: It can't, because harvested water just stays in tanks.

misconceptions.root_belief: one thing has only one purpose

misconceptions.statement: My water footprint is only the water I drink and use for bathing.
misconceptions.why: Students count only the water they directly see being used.
misconceptions.fix: Water footprint includes direct use plus the water used to produce food, clothes and other things we use.

probe.question: Does the water used to grow your rice count in your water footprint?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only water from my taps counts.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
misconceptions.source_hint: studies on students' understanding of hidden/virtual water and resource footprints

misconceptions.statement: Making a cotton T-shirt or a kilogram of rice uses only a few litres of water.
misconceptions.why: Students think only of the water visible in the final product.
misconceptions.fix: Producing cotton, rice and many goods takes thousands of litres of water, mostly for growing the crops.

probe.question: About how much water is needed to produce one T-shirt?
probe.wrong_answer: A few litres, about a bucketful.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

misconceptions.statement: A slowly dripping tap wastes so little water that it does not matter.
misconceptions.why: Each drop looks tiny, so students ignore it adding up over time.
misconceptions.fix: A dripping tap can waste dozens of litres a day and thousands of litres in a year.

probe.question: A tap drips 1 drop every second, with each drop about 0.05 mL. Is the waste important?
probe.wrong_answer: No, drops are tiny, so it makes no real difference.

misconceptions.root_belief: small things do not add up
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of children's reasoning about small repeated quantities and resource waste

misconceptions.statement: Leaving the tap running while brushing teeth does not waste water since the water goes down the drain and returns to nature.
misconceptions.why: Students think used water just goes back to the water cycle for free.
misconceptions.fix: Running water wastes treated, clean water which cost energy and effort to supply; closing the tap saves many litres each time.

probe.question: Does it matter if you keep the tap on while brushing?
probe.wrong_answer: No, the water just goes back to nature anyway.

misconceptions.root_belief: nature always restores what we use

misconceptions.statement: Saving water is the job of adults and the government, not students.
misconceptions.why: Students think large systems decide water use.
misconceptions.fix: Small daily habits in homes and schools add up to large savings, so everyone's actions count.

probe.question: Can a student's habits change how much water a school uses?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only adults and the government can.

misconceptions.root_belief: my small action has no effect

misconceptions.statement: Water used for washing clothes or vegetables is useless and must be thrown away.
misconceptions.why: Students think used water is dirty and has no further use.
misconceptions.fix: Such greywater can often be reused for mopping, flushing or watering plants, though not for drinking.

probe.question: What can we do with the water left after washing vegetables?
probe.wrong_answer: Throw it away because it can't be used again.

misconceptions.root_belief: used means finished

misconceptions.statement: Drip irrigation gives plants more water than flooding the field.
misconceptions.why: Students think better watering means more water.
misconceptions.fix: Drip irrigation gives smaller, targeted amounts at the roots, saving water and often giving equal or better yields.

probe.question: Does drip irrigation use more water than flooding a field?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it gives plants much more water.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

misconceptions.statement: Water that runs off or evaporates from a field is not really lost, since it goes back to the water cycle.
misconceptions.why: Students see the water cycle as instant and local.
misconceptions.fix: Evaporated or runoff water leaves the farm and is no longer available to the crop or local wells; it may fall elsewhere later.

probe.question: Is water lost by evaporation from a flooded field a real loss for the farmer?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it returns to the cycle so nothing is lost.

misconceptions.root_belief: nature always restores what we use
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of children's ideas on the water cycle

misconceptions.statement: Watering plants at noon in strong sun is best because the sun helps them drink.
misconceptions.why: Students link sun with plant growth and so with watering.
misconceptions.fix: Watering in early morning or evening loses less water to evaporation, so more reaches the roots.

probe.question: When is the best time to water plants?
probe.wrong_answer: At noon, when the sun is strongest.

misconceptions.root_belief: more of a helpful thing is always better
